core.p: If you follow the concentration of a reactant (for example by titration or with a sensor), the curve falls; for a product it rises. The same rules apply: gradient = rate, flat = reaction finished.
bullets: Reactant concentration falls steeply at first and then levels off (at zero if it is the limiting reactant, or above zero if it is in excess).
Product concentration rises steeply at first and then levels off.
Rate units: mol/dm3 per second (mol dm^-3 s^-1) or g/dm3 per second.
The reactant curve and product curve are related by the equation: if 1 mol of reactant makes 1 mol of product, one falls as fast as the other rises.

core.p: You may be asked to plot results then draw a line of best fit. Accuracy here earns easy marks.
bullets: Use a scale that makes the points cover **more than half** of the grid in each direction.
Label both axes with the quantity and the **unit**, for example 'Volume of gas / cm3' and 'Time / s'.
Plot points accurately with small neat crosses.
Draw a **smooth curve of best fit** through or close to the points; do not join dot to dot.
Identify **anomalous** results that do not fit the pattern and ignore them when drawing the curve.
The curve should go through the origin for a product (no product at time zero).

callouts.p: Joining each point with straight ruler lines loses the line of best fit mark. Rate graphs are smooth curves.

core.h: Explaining differences between curves using collision theory
core.p: A full answer links the graph feature to the particle explanation. The graph shows WHAT happens; collision theory explains WHY.
bullets: Steeper curve at higher temperature: particles move faster, collide more frequently and a greater proportion of collisions have at least the activation energy.
Steeper curve at higher concentration: more particles in the same volume, so more frequent collisions.
Steeper curve with powder: larger surface area to volume ratio, so more frequent collisions.
Steeper curve with a catalyst: an alternative pathway with lower activation energy.
Same final height: the same amount of limiting reactant, so the same amount of product.

callouts.p: For 'compare the curves' questions write one sentence about the gradient (rate) and one about the final height (amount of product).

analogy.t: Filling a bucket from a water butt
analogy.p: Imagine filling a bucket from a water butt that is emptying. At first the butt is full, the pressure is high and water gushes out fast, so the bucket's water level rises steeply. As the butt empties, the flow slows and the level rises more gently. When the butt is empty the level stays flat. The steepness of the 'water level against time' graph is the flow rate, just as the gradient of a volume-time graph is the rate of reaction, and the final level is set by how much water was in the butt (the limiting reactant). Where it breaks down: the water flow slows because of falling pressure, whereas a reaction slows because fewer reactant particles mean less frequent collisions.

terms.d: The change in amount of reactant or product per unit time; the gradient of an amount-time graph.
The steepness of a line: change in y divided by change in x.
Total change in quantity divided by the time taken; the gradient of a straight line between two points on the curve.
A straight line that touches a curve at one point and has the same gradient as the curve at that point.
The rate at the very start of the reaction (t = 0); the fastest rate, found from a tangent at the origin.
The gradient of the tangent to the curve at that time (Higher tier).
The point where the curve becomes horizontal, showing the reaction has stopped.
The reactant used up first; it decides when the reaction stops and how much product forms.
A smooth line or curve drawn close to as many points as possible, showing the overall trend.
A result that does not fit the pattern of the others.
The variable plotted on the x-axis; here, time.
The variable plotted on the y-axis; the quantity measured, such as volume of gas.
Lines drawn on a graph from the axis to the curve to read off values.
The point (0,0) where the axes meet; product curves start here.

mistakes.w: The flat part of the graph shows the reaction is slow.
mistakes.r: The flat part shows the reaction has **stopped** because a reactant (the limiting reactant) has been **used up**.

mistakes.w: The rate is the highest point on the graph.
mistakes.r: The rate is the **gradient** of the graph; the highest point is the **total amount of product**.

mistakes.w: A catalyst makes the curve finish higher.
mistakes.r: A catalyst makes the curve **steeper** but it levels off at the **same final height**.

mistakes.w: The reaction slows down because the particles get tired / lose energy.
mistakes.r: It slows down because reactants are **used up**, so there are fewer particles and **less frequent collisions**.

mistakes.w: Rate at 20 s = volume at 20 s / 20.
mistakes.r: That gives the **mean rate** over the first 20 s; the rate **at** 20 s is the gradient of the **tangent** at 20 s.

mistakes.w: Joining all the plotted points with a ruler.
mistakes.r: Draw a **smooth curve of best fit**, ignoring anomalous points.

mistakes.w: Sketched faster curve not starting at zero.
mistakes.r: Any product curve must **start at the origin** because no product exists at time zero.

mistakes.w: Using points on the curve to calculate a tangent's gradient.
mistakes.r: Read both corners of the triangle from the **tangent line** itself, using a large triangle.

exam.q: State how the rate of reaction can be found from a graph of volume of gas against time.
model: From the gradient/slope of the graph (steeper = faster).
exam.tip: Gradient is the key word.

exam.q: Explain why the graph of volume of gas against time becomes horizontal.
model: The reaction has stopped / no more gas is produced.
Because one reactant (limiting reactant) has been used up.
exam.tip: Give both what happens and why.

exam.q: A reaction produced 75 cm3 of gas in total and finished after 150 s. Calculate the mean rate of reaction.
model: Mean rate = 75 / 150.
exam.tip: Always include units.

exam.q: Describe how the rate of reaction changes during the reaction, as shown by a volume of gas against time curve.
model: Rate is fastest at the start (steepest).
Rate decreases (gradient falls) until it is zero when the line is flat.
exam.tip: Use the words 'steep' and 'gradient'.

exam.q: Explain, using collision theory, why the gradient of the curve decreases as the reaction proceeds.
model: Reactant particles are used up.
Concentration of reactants decreases / fewer particles in the same volume.
So collisions are less frequent, so the rate decreases.
exam.tip: Link fewer particles to less frequent collisions.

exam.q: On the same axes as curve A, sketch the curve you would expect if the experiment was repeated at a higher temperature with the same amounts of reactants.
model: Curve starts at origin and is steeper than A initially.
Levels off at the same final volume as A (and sooner).
exam.tip: Two features to show: steeper start, same final height.

exam.q: The experiment was repeated with half the mass of magnesium (magnesium is the limiting reactant), all other conditions the same. Describe how the new curve compares with the original.
model: Levels off at half the final volume.
Initial gradient is less steep / reaction slower (smaller surface area of magnesium).
exam.tip: Halving the limiting reactant halves the total product.

exam.q: Higher: Describe how you would use the graph to find the rate of reaction at 30 s.
model: Draw a tangent to the curve at 30 s.
Draw a (large) triangle on the tangent and read the change in y and change in x.
Rate = change in y / change in x (gradient of the tangent).
exam.tip: Mention 'tangent' and 'gradient'.

exam.q: Higher: A tangent drawn at 20 s passes through (0 s, 10 cm3) and (40 s, 58 cm3). Calculate the rate of reaction at 20 s.
exam.tip: Subtract in the same order on top and bottom.

exam.q: Two experiments were carried out with marble chips and excess hydrochloric acid: one with large chips and one with the same mass of small chips. Their volume-time graphs are drawn on the same axes. Describe and explain the differences between the two curves.
model: Small chips curve has a steeper initial gradient, showing a faster rate.
Small chips curve levels off sooner (reaction finishes in less time).
Both curves level off at the same final volume.
Small chips have a larger surface area to volume ratio, so more particles are exposed to acid.
So collisions are more frequent, giving more successful collisions per second.
Same mass of calcium carbonate (limiting reactant), so same amount of carbon dioxide produced.
exam.tip: Describe gradient, finish time and final height, then explain each one.

exam.q: A graph shows the mass of a flask and its contents falling from 85.40 g to 84.20 g, after which it stays constant. State the mass of carbon dioxide produced.
exam.tip: Mass lost = mass of gas given off.

worked.q: Hydrogen gas volumes: 0 s 0 cm3; 20 s 30 cm3; 40 s 48 cm3; 60 s 57 cm3; 80 s 60 cm3; 100 s 60 cm3. (a) When did the reaction stop? (b) Calculate the mean rate over the first 20 s and between 40 s and 60 s. (c) Calculate the mean rate for the whole reaction.
steps: (a) The volume first reaches its constant value of 60 cm3 at 80 s, so the reaction stopped at (or just before) 80 s.
The later rate is smaller because reactants have been used up, so collisions are less frequent.
(c) Whole reaction: 60 cm3 / 80 s = 0.75 cm3/s.
worked.ans: (a) About 80 s. (b) 1.5 cm3/s, then 0.45 cm3/s. (c) 0.75 cm3/s.

worked.q: Higher: A tangent is drawn to a volume-time curve at 50 s. Two points on the tangent are (10 s, 20 cm3) and (90 s, 68 cm3). Calculate the rate of reaction at 50 s.
steps: Change in y = 68 - 20 = 48 cm3.
Change in x = 90 - 10 = 80 s.
Gradient = 48 / 80 = 0.60.
The gradient of the tangent equals the rate at that time.

worked.q: Model answer: a graph shows curve P for 1.0 mol/dm3 acid and curve Q for 0.5 mol/dm3 acid (same volume, acid is the limiting reactant, magnesium in excess). Explain why Q is less steep and finishes at half the volume of P.
steps: Q has a lower concentration, so fewer acid particles in the same volume.
So collisions are less frequent and the rate is slower: smaller initial gradient.
Q contains half the number of moles of acid (the limiting reactant).
So only half as much hydrogen can be made: the curve levels off at half the height.
worked.ans: Q is less steep because of less frequent collisions at lower concentration, and reaches half the final volume because it contains half the amount of the limiting reactant.
